The D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} seed acquires no anomalous dimension at this order: its plaquette selector lies entirely in the SO(5) representation 𝟑𝟓\mathbf{35} as a Lorentz vector, an eigenspace with Δ=4\Delta=4 at O⁡(1/N)O(1/N), whose anomalous graphs cancel (Appendix K) and which cannot mix with operators containing gauge or Higgs fields. Its remaining half, a vector 𝟓\mathbf{5} with Lorentz spin 2 at Δ=3.91\Delta=3.91, carries no QBT channel. The isotropic VBS attraction it competes with does run. Its rank-2-tensor part has Δ=3.46\Delta=3.46 and grows by a factor of 4040–100100 over LL relative to the seed. Its SO(5)-singlet scalar part grows fastest. Unlike in QED3, in SU(2) the current square does not represent Fa​FaF^{a}F^{a}. For the π\pi-flux SU(2) state, which the fermions alone screen, the four-fermion block yields the singlet instability found in Ref. [129], and the dimension of Fa​FaF^{a}F^{a} removes it at O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) (Appendix K). At the multicritical point the O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) mixing problem of the channel is solved in Appendix K. At N=∞N=\infty it contains five operators of dimension four that are SO(5) and O(2) singlets, Lorentz scalars and even under 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒯\mathcal{T}: (Tr​𝒳¯​𝒳)2(\mathrm{Tr}\,\bar{\mathcal{X}}\mathcal{X})^{2}; the square R=J⟂a​J⟂aR=J^{a}_{\perp}J^{a}_{\perp} of the relative current J⟂=xb​Jψ−xf​JΦJ_{\perp}=x_{b}J_{\psi}-x_{f}J_{\Phi}, which the gauge-field equation of motion makes equal to Jψ2J_{\psi}^{2}, JΦ2J_{\Phi}^{2} and −Jψ⋅JΦ-J_{\psi}\cdot J_{\Phi}, with xbx_{b} and xf=1−xbx_{f}=1-x_{b} the Higgs and fermion shares of the screening; Fa​FaF^{a}F^{a}, whose O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) dimension with fermion and Higgs loops is ΓF​F=5.14\Gamma_{FF}=5.14 [Eq. (42)]; σ2\sigma^{2}, with σ\sigma the constraint field of the Higgs sector; and the square of the covariant gradient of the gauge-spin-2 Higgs bilinear. The lowest mode dominated by the four-fermion operators has Δ1=2.99\Delta_{1}=2.99 (2.912.91 in the physical-NfN_{f} counting), independent of the gauge parameter, so the lowest four-fermion singlet is relevant, or close to marginal, at this order, as is the lowest singlet of the SO(5) deconfined point on the fuzzy sphere [137], although the two values are not quantitatively comparable (Appendix K). The channel also contains a mode that is 92%92\% σ2\sigma^{2}, at Δ=0.46\Delta=0.46. The constraint field has Δσ=2−72​u=0.38\Delta_{\sigma}=2-72u=0.38 at N=12N=12, with u=8/(3​π2​N)u=8/(3\pi^{2}N) [Eq. (31) of Sec. VII], below the unitarity bound 1/21/2 [80, 25], because the adjoint Higgs field carries the Casimir 88 against 33 for the fermions, so the 1/N1/N expansion of the Higgs sector is not controlled at N=12N=12. We therefore scan Δσ\Delta_{\sigma}. For Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} between 0.380.38 and 1.51.5, Δ1\Delta_{1} lies between 2.992.99 and 3.243.24 (2.912.91 and 3.183.18), and for Δσ=1.75\Delta_{\sigma}=1.75–22 the level ordering changes and the lowest four-fermion-dominated mode lies at 2.472.47–2.652.65. The two further Higgs operators of the channel, σ​Tr​M~2\sigma\,\mathrm{Tr}\,\tilde{M}^{2} and (Tr​M~2)2(\mathrm{Tr}\,\tilde{M}^{2})^{2}, decouple at this order. Their mixing with the five operators is at most of order N−3/2N^{-3/2} in the normalized basis, since the graphs of lower order are scaleless, vanish by the tracelessness of M~a​b\tilde{M}_{ab} or are removed by the equation of motion, and it moves Δ1\Delta_{1} only at O⁡(1/N2)O(1/N^{2}) (Appendix K).

The seeds at λ\lambda follow from the full matrix. At the O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) value of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} the σ2\sigma^{2} mode dominates the running, and the fractional anisotropy at λ\lambda is reduced from 0.040.04–0.080.08 to 10−1310^{-13}–10−1010^{-10}; over the scan of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} up to 22 it stays below 10−510^{-5}, and the vertex asymmetry of the QBT flow below Δ​ln⁡Γ≃10−4\Delta\ln\Gamma\simeq 10^{-4}. If a single dimension Δ1≃3\Delta_{1}\simeq 3 is instead assigned to the four-fermion singlet, the fractional anisotropy reaches a few times 10−510^{-5} and the asymmetry 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} (Appendices K and L). In every variant the flow ends on the VBS ray and the D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} seed keeps its sign. The VBS and Néelz couplings keep their tree-level signs, whereas the flux coupling, repulsive at tree level, becomes attractive at λ\lambda in the leading counting for every Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} of the scan, and in the physical-NfN_{f} counting for Δσ≤1.75\Delta_{\sigma}\leq 1.75, because the lowest four-fermion-dominated mode is dominated by the current square, which carries the same sign in all three channels. Below λ\lambda the screened gauge interaction of Sec. X.1 adds a valley-blind VBS attraction, which dilutes the anisotropy further and keeps its sign. At the material couplings (d≃0.007d\simeq 0.007–0.0150.015) the fractional anisotropy of the determinant in the band-touching channel is 1.8×10−71.8\times 10^{-7}–8.1×10−78.1\times 10^{-7}, and the full ratio b2/Δ​Fisob_{2}/\Delta F_{\rm iso} is smaller; the Wick term of D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} in the determinant, which also favors PfP_{\rm f} for D⟂′<0D^{\prime}_{\perp}<0, contributes about 10−1010^{-10}–10−910^{-9}. If a single dimension Δ1\Delta_{1} is assigned to the four-fermion singlet, with the rank-2 part of the attraction at Δ=3.46\Delta=3.46, the D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} seed leads the determinant only if Δ1\Delta_{1} exceeds a crossover value Δ1∗=1.90\Delta_{1}^{*}=1.90–2.212.21 at L=7L=7 and 2.272.27–2.522.52 at L=8.5L=8.5 with b2/Δ​Fisob_{2}/\Delta F_{\rm iso}, the consistent choice at the gap-equation saddle, or 2.252.25–2.472.47 and 2.562.56–2.742.74 with A/CisoA/C_{\rm iso} (for |D⟂′|=0.10|D^{\prime}_{\perp}|=0.10 meV, about 0.080.08 lower for 0.180.18 meV); if the rank-2 tensor is instead relevant, as on the fuzzy sphere, that part of the attraction grows by a larger factor and the seed never leads. With the full matrix, in the leading counting, the seed leads only for Δσ≳1.5\Delta_{\sigma}\gtrsim 1.5 (1.751.75) at L=7L=7 with the first (second) ratio, and at L=8.5L=8.5 only for Δσ≳1.75\Delta_{\sigma}\gtrsim 1.75 with the first and for no Δσ≤2\Delta_{\sigma}\leq 2 with the second; at the O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) value of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} the determinant leads. The direction of the DM correction is therefore not determined at O⁡(1/N)O(1/N): where the seed leads it favors, for D⟂′<0D^{\prime}_{\perp}<0, the full plaquette, and where the determinant leads it favors the empty one. After the running the DM correction is in every case a small bias, the flow ends on the VBS ray, and the pattern that forms is decided by the pure-model term unless that term is smaller still.

XI Magnetic field: direction-selective mass activation

Classifying the 36 operators under the stabilizer of (DM,𝑩)(\text{DM},\bm{B}), the locked elements OO with O​𝑩=𝑩O\bm{B}=\bm{B} and the products 𝒯​O\mathcal{T}O with O​𝑩=−𝑩O\bm{B}=-\bm{B}, gives Table 6. There NaN^{a} denotes the Néel mass along the crystal axis aa, the continuum image of the staggered magnetization ∑iϵi​Sia\sum_{i}\epsilon_{i}S_{i}^{a} with ϵi=+1\epsilon_{i}=+1 on the [110][110] dimers and −1-1 on the [1​1¯​0][1\bar{1}0] dimers. Field and moment directions refer to crystal axes, related to the spin labels of Tables 2–4 as stated in Appendix A.

The stabilizer analysis determines which masses are allowed. The leading power follows separately. The field induces an effective staggered field, a term linear in the Néel order parameter. It is 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd and appears at linear order in BB. Their order in the DM couplings follows from σ^h=𝟙⊗C2​z\hat{\sigma}_{h}=\mathds{1}\otimes C_{2z}, which acts on the layer as the global spin rotation C2​zC_{2z}. It maps the model with in-plane DM components, the out-of-plane components D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} and the field 𝑩\bm{B} exactly onto the model with the in-plane components reversed, the same D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} and the field C2​z​𝑩C_{2z}\bm{B}, and it reverses the in-plane components of 𝑵\bm{N}. An in-plane staggered field linear in an in-plane field is therefore even in the in-plane DM couplings, and the term of first order is forbidden. The locked group of the high-temperature structure, which contains σ^h\hat{\sigma}_{h} and so classifies the terms of even order, keeps the tensor Nx∝ByN^{x}\propto B_{y}, Ny∝BxN^{y}\propto B_{x} of Table 6. The leading order is thus the second, λ​D\lambda D at the Gaussian level computed below, where here and in Table 6 DD denotes the in-plane inter-dimer source D′∥,sD^{\prime}_{\parallel,s}, not the intra-dimer DD. With D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} alone the model keeps the spin rotations about cc, and no staggered field appears at any order. Within the spin model the staggered field is therefore of second order in spin–orbit coupling. A dependence of the in-plane gg tensor on the dimer orientation, which the Cu site symmetry allows and the model omits, enters at first order. With in-plane components g1g_{1} along the dimer and g2g_{2} across it, the Zeeman term μB​∑i𝑩⋅gi​𝑺i\mu_{B}\sum_{i}\bm{B}\cdot g_{i}\bm{S}_{i}, gig_{i} being the gg tensor of site ii, contains 12​(g1−g2)​μB​∑iϵi​(By​Six+Bx​Siy)\frac{1}{2}(g_{1}-g_{2})\mu_{B}\sum_{i}\epsilon_{i}(B_{y}S_{i}^{x}+B_{x}S_{i}^{y}). This is a staggered field with the same tensor, and we do not estimate g1−g2g_{1}-g_{2}. An alternating gg tensor and DM interactions together generate the staggered field behind the field-induced gap of the spin chain Cu benzoate [89], the one-dimensional precedent of this mechanism. The field conjugate to the valence-bond imbalance is 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even and must be even in 𝑩\bm{B}, and for [110][110] its leading form is Bx​ByB_{x}B_{y} times a DM-even coefficient. Since Vx−Vy=−PfV_{x}-V_{y}=-P_{\rm f} (Sec. X.3), it is a full-plaquette field, of opposite sign for [110][110] and [1​1¯​0][1\bar{1}0]. At order B2B^{2} and at the mean-field (Gaussian) level that coefficient receives contributions from three channels. The single-particle channel is the Zeeman term on the 16 zero modes with the DM-split QBT multiplet as intermediate space (second-order Schrieffer–Wolff). The second channel is the Hartree–Fock (Wick) response of HDMH_{\rm DM}, and the third is the Hartree–Fock response of the Heisenberg quartics J′J^{\prime} (NN) and JJ (dimer). The last two are evaluated on the field-polarized thermal Gaussian state of the π\pi-flux ansatz including the Wick-induced DM operator (d=0.6d=0.6, T=0.5​tT=0.5t on an 828^{2} torus, comparable to its finite-size single-particle gap 0.46​t0.46t, magnetization linear in BB). This temperature exceeds 4​λ≃0.2​t4\lambda\simeq 0.2t at d=0.6d=0.6, so the magnitudes and signs of the Gaussian coefficients below are those of a high-temperature state and are not computed below T∗T^{*}. The orders in BB and in the DM couplings are analytic statements and do not depend on this choice. The single-particle channel gives no VBS-imbalance mass at O⁡(B2)O(B^{2}), only the spin-current anisotropies Jx​σx−Jy​σyJ^{x}\sigma^{x}-J^{y}\sigma^{y} ([100][100]) and Jx​σy+Jy​σxJ^{x}\sigma^{y}+J^{y}\sigma^{x} ([110][110]), in the spin labels of the tables. On a DM-free Gaussian state the Wick channel gives none either. With the DM operator in the state the mean-field responses follow the symmetry table. For 𝑩|[100]\bm{B}\parallel[100] the DM channel produces the Néel mass NyN^{y} linear in BB and no VBS imbalance. For 𝑩|[110]\bm{B}\parallel[110] it produces (Nx+Ny)/2(N^{x}+N^{y})/\sqrt{2}, the Néel component along 𝑩\bm{B}, linear in BB, and the VBS imbalance Vx−VyV_{x}-V_{y} at order B2B^{2} (coefficient −1.6×10−5-1.6\times 10^{-5} per unit DD at B=0.2​tB=0.2t). Both Néel coefficients are ∝B​λ​D\propto B\lambda D, of second order in the in-plane DM couplings as the σ^h\hat{\sigma}_{h} argument requires. They change sign with λ\lambda at fixed DD and are linear in BB and in λ\lambda. The NN exchange channel adds an O⁡(B2)O(B^{2}) imbalance of −1.1×10−6-1.1\times 10^{-6} per unit J′J^{\prime}, and the dimer exchange adds none. Since the imbalance vanishes when the DM operator is removed from the state, it is of second order in the DM couplings. The DM-channel coefficient scales linearly with dd and the exchange-channel one quadratically, so Vx−Vy∝B2​λ​DV_{x}-V_{y}\propto B^{2}\lambda D and B2​λ2​J′B^{2}\lambda^{2}J^{\prime}. At the mean-field level the imbalance is smaller than the Néel activation by a factor ∝B\propto B (ratio 0.070.07 at B=0.2​tB=0.2t for the unit-normalized combinations (Vx−Vy)/2(V_{x}-V_{y})/\sqrt{2} and (Nx+Ny)/2(N^{x}+N^{y})/\sqrt{2}). Fluctuation corrections beyond the Gaussian decoupling are not computed. The symmetry statement, even in 𝑩\bm{B} and allowed as Bx​ByB_{x}B_{y}, holds independently of the decoupling. For 𝑩|[001]\bm{B}\parallel[001] the single-particle channel confirms the locking of Sec. IX.2. The Zeeman term projects on the QBT onto the flux mass alone, linear in BB with no O⁡(B2)O(B^{2}) remainder and with the same coefficient for both signs of λ\lambda, and it gaps the QBT modes at Γ\Gamma to g​μB​B/2g\mu_{B}B/2, the lowest spinon excitation (a spin flip costs g​μB​Bg\mu_{B}B). The coefficient carries no factor of λ\lambda, but the coupling requires spin–orbit locking. Without spin–orbit coupling MzM_{z} belongs to a spin triplet and cannot couple linearly to the flux mass, a spin singlet. On the lattice (d=0.3d=0.3 and 0.60.6) the field-induced gap is linear for g​μB​B/2≲0.1×4​λg\mu_{B}B/2\lesssim 0.1\times 4\lambda and saturates near 0.4×4​λ0.4\times 4\lambda, and CBdGC_{\rm BdG} is unchanged up to g​μB​B/2=2.5×4​λg\mu_{B}B/2=2.5\times 4\lambda (Appendix J).

The field-induced Néel moment for an in-plane field is to be distinguished from the staggered magnetization that the intra-dimer DM interaction and the staggered gg tensor induce in the dimer phase [63, 82, 81]. The buckling tilts the principal gg axes alternately toward the ⟨110⟩\langle 110\rangle directions and allows the intra-dimer DM coupling. Both mix the dimer singlet with the lowest triplet at first order, whereas an inter-dimer DM coupling, which acts on two dimers, has no matrix element between the singlet product state and a single-triplet state [82, 115]. The dimer-phase staggered moment therefore does not measure, at leading order, the in-plane inter-dimer couplings that set λ\lambda. In the two geometries of Ref. [63], the induced intra-dimer staggered moments lie in-plane along each dimer’s own axis for 𝑩|[001]\bm{B}\parallel[001] and along cc on the dimers parallel to the field for 𝑩|[110]\bm{B}\parallel[110]. The two responses differ in two ways. In both geometries one of field and moment lies in the plane and the other along cc. Under σ^h\hat{\sigma}_{h} those moments are therefore odd in the in-plane couplings and appear at first order in DD and gsg_{s}, whereas the Néel response to an in-plane field is even. They are intra-dimer staggered moments of the gapped dimer phase and differ from the (π,π)(\pi,\pi) Néel masses of Table 6. For 𝑩|[001]\bm{B}\parallel[001] their in-plane dimer-staggered moment is compatible with our classification only in the weaker sense that the Néel mass channel is forbidden there while staggered spatial-current channels remain allowed. A positive identification of the observed response with a specific allowed channel requires a matrix-element calculation we do not perform. The [100][100] prediction has no measured counterpart.

The critical scaling of the [100][100] response is ms∝B​𝒟​ξ 3−2​ΔNm_{s}\propto B\,\mathcal{D}\,\xi^{\,3-2\Delta_{N}}, with 𝒟\mathcal{D} the coupling factor of the source, λD′∥,s\lambda D^{\prime}_{\parallel,s} at mean field or g1−g2g_{1}-g_{2}. That scaling is the singular part, and a regular ultraviolet contribution coexists with it. With the leading-order value ΔN=ΔV=1.46\Delta_{N}=\Delta_{V}=1.46 of Sec. VII the exponent is 3−2​ΔN=+0.083-2\Delta_{N}=+0.08, so the [100][100] Néel response is weakly enhanced at criticality. An exponent this small leaves the regular contribution able to dominate the total response over accessible ranges of ξ\xi. The leading-order value fixes only the sign of the exponent (Sec. VII). For the much smaller ΔN\Delta_{N} found in numerics on the bosonic deconfined quantum critical point (DQCP) [86] the exponent would be of order one and the response strongly enhanced, itself a diagnostic of the anomalous dimension. The sharp prediction is the orientation selectivity of the Néel response, which is symmetry-activated for 𝑩|[100]\bm{B}\parallel[100] and symmetry-forbidden for 𝑩|[001]\bm{B}\parallel[001]. The test is 11B NMR at 2.42.4–2.82.8 GPa comparing 𝑩|[100]\bm{B}\parallel[100] with 𝑩|[001]\bm{B}\parallel[001] at matched Zeeman energy g​μB​Bg\mu_{B}B, below the field-induced transition near 5.55.5–5.75.7 T, provided the in-plane staggered moment transfers a nonzero hyperfine field to the boron site; the existing data do not make this comparison (Sec. XIII.2). A cc-axis field also splits the lines, through the intra-dimer staggered moments, so the test is the pattern of the splitting, a Néel pattern, with the two moments of each dimer parallel, for [100][100] and none for [001][001] at the same g​μB​Bg\mu_{B}B, measured above the plaquette ordering temperature. Exact diagonalization of Eq. (1) with the I​4¯​2​mI\bar{4}2m DM vectors on 16-, 20- and 8-site clusters, the last at finite temperature, confirms the rule independently of the gauge theory: the linear response is (Nx,Ny)∝(By,Bx)(N^{x},N^{y})\propto(B_{y},B_{x}), even and quadratic in the in-plane couplings, absent for D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} alone and for 𝑩|c\bm{B}\parallel c, with a sign that depends on J′/JJ^{\prime}/J and TT (Appendix M). The selection rule follows from the lattice symmetry and holds in the dimer phase as well. Only the dependence of the [100][100] response on the distance to the critical pressure is specific to the spin-liquid regime. It is weak at leading order in 1/N1/N and strong if ΔN\Delta_{N} is as small as in bosonic-DQCP numerics [86]. We quote no number for the size of the staggered moment, because the Gaussian coefficient is a mean-field estimate whose fluctuation corrections are not computed, and we do not estimate g1−g2g_{1}-g_{2}.

Tilted fields. The same tensor bears on field-tuned tests of deconfined criticality. Any in-plane component of the field, as in a field tilted by θ\theta from cc, is linearly conjugate to the in-plane Néel order parameter, with the same magnitude for every azimuth. For a general azimuth it removes every symmetry that distinguishes the field-induced antiferromagnet from the paramagnet; for a tilt within a {100}\{100\}–cc or {110}\{110\}–cc plane a twofold symmetry survives. Only a field strictly along cc keeps the full Néel symmetry. The conjugate staggered field, hs∼12​(g1−g2)​μB​B​sin⁡θh_{s}\sim\tfrac{1}{2}(g_{1}-g_{2})\mu_{B}B\sin\theta plus a term of second order in the in-plane DM couplings, is relevant with RG eigenvalue 3−ΔN3-\Delta_{N} and rounds a critical point on the scale Th∼Λ​(hs/Λ)1/(3−ΔN)T_{h}\sim\Lambda(h_{s}/\Lambda)^{1/(3-\Delta_{N})}. For an illustrative |g1−g2|=10−2|g_{1}-g_{2}|=10^{-2}, the 8.6∘8.6^{\circ} tilt of Ref. [20] at Hc≃5.7H_{c}\simeq 5.7 T and a cutoff Λ≃J′\Lambda\simeq J^{\prime}–J≃50J\simeq 50–8585 K give Th∼0.1T_{h}\sim 0.1 K at the large-NN value ΔN=1.46\Delta_{N}=1.46 and ∼1\sim 1 K at ΔN≃0.63\Delta_{N}\simeq 0.63, the value implied by the loop-model estimate ηN​e´​el≃0.26\eta_{\rm N\acute{e}el}\simeq 0.26 [86]. The sharp ordering signatures reported with that tilt therefore bound |g1−g2||g_{1}-g_{2}| from above if ΔN\Delta_{N} is small.

XII Quenched disorder

Pressure and strain inhomogeneity make quenched randomness integral to the SrCu2(BO3)2 phase diagram. Its effect on the theory above is fixed by two inputs from the operator tables, the 𝒯\mathcal{T} parities of the 36 operators and their dimensions. Non-magnetic disorder preserves 𝒯\mathcal{T} in every realization while breaking lattice symmetries locally, so it couples random fields to every 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even local operator and to no 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd one. Exchange randomness δ​J\delta J (spin-singlet, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even) couples linearly to the VBS doublet (Vx,Vy)(V_{x},V_{y}) and to the valley currents. Random DM δ​D\delta D couples to the spin currents, as a random λ⁡(𝒓)\lambda(\bm{r}), and to the 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even staggered spin-current densities γ0​μx,z​σa\gamma^{0}\mu^{x,z}\sigma^{a}. Being 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even, these densities are not magnetization-like. Their natural microscopic content is staggered vector-chirality and spin-current textures, the operators that DM itself conjugates. No randomness couples linearly to the flux mass or to the Néel masses. Chirality and magnetism are random-field protected by 𝒯\mathcal{T}, and the VBS is not. Beyond the 36 fermion bilinears, the critical Higgs sector adds gauge-invariant 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even bilinears at the multicritical point, where N=12N=12 and the eigenvalue yΔ=1.08y_{\Delta}=1.08 below is defined: Φ1⋅Φ1+Φ2⋅Φ2\Phi_{1}\cdot\Phi_{1}+\Phi_{2}\cdot\Phi_{2}, the tuning parameter, to which bond randomness couples as a random TcT_{c}, and Φ1⋅Φ1−Φ2⋅Φ2\Phi_{1}\cdot\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\cdot\Phi_{2} and Φ1⋅Φ2\Phi_{1}\cdot\Phi_{2}, which break the lattice symmetry and receive random fields. Their dimensions, derived below, are not controlled at N=12N=12, and they are 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even, so they do not affect the protection of chirality, but random TcT_{c} and random Higgs-anisotropy fields may well dominate at the multicritical point.

Disorder in SrCu2(BO3)2 and its strength. Four sources of quenched randomness are documented. (i) Point defects that free a spin 1/21/2: low-temperature Curie tails correspond to 0.14%0.14\% of free spins per Cu in traveling-solvent floating-zone crystals [56] and to 0.70.7–1%1\% in powders [55, 107]. Substitution does not leave only spinless vacancies: Mg on the Cu site and La or Na on the Sr site each prevent a dimer singlet from forming and free a Cu spin 1/21/2 [1], Mg at 2.5%2.5\% of the Cu sites leaves unpaired spins 1/21/2 antiferromagnetically correlated with the surrounding singlets [41], 11B NMR on Zn-doped crystals images an extended spin polaron around each Zn [132], and Mg incorporation in solid-state synthesis levels off near x≈0.05x\approx 0.05–0.070.07 in SrCu2-xMgx(BO3)2 [107]. (ii) Inversion twins, formed at TsT_{s} as incoherent microtwins of equal volume fraction and, according to Ref. [112], presumably with high wall concentrations; their size has not been measured. They reverse every in-plane DM component [113], while JJ, J′J^{\prime} and D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp}, which are allowed above TsT_{s}, are the same in both twins. (iii) Pressure gradients. All pressure media are solid or glassy at the measurement temperatures [116]: Daphne 7373 is solid at room temperature above 2.22.2 GPa, with solidification setting in near 2.02.0 GPa [131], and in a diamond-anvil-cell survey of fourteen media non-hydrostatic effects (ruby-line broadening from pressure gradients and uniaxial stress) developed in all of them at low temperature, weakest for helium, nitrogen and argon [116]. The narrow coexistence of the plaquette and antiferromagnetic phases, which Ref. [39] attributes to a tiny pressure inhomogeneity, suggests an in situ spread of about δ​P≈0.02\delta P\approx 0.02–0.050.05 GPa; Ref. [20] attributes its own dimer–plaquette coexistence to the slope of the first-order line. This spread corresponds to δ⁡(J′/J)≈(0.6CLOSE\delta(J^{\prime}/J)\approx(0.6–OPEN1.6)×10−31.6)\times 10^{-3} with d⁡(J′/J)/d​P≃0.032d(J^{\prime}/J)/dP\simeq 0.032 GPa-1 [96]. (iv) Shear strain from non-hydrostatic stress and dislocations, not measured and plausibly 10−510^{-5}–10−310^{-3}. These sources enter the classification above differently. A hydrostatic gradient is fully symmetric and acts as random-TcT_{c} disorder, not as a random VBS field. The two plaquette states differ in symmetry: a full-plaquette order that is the same in all layers transforms like ϵx​y\epsilon_{xy} (irrep B2B_{2} of 4¯​2​m\bar{4}2m; F​m​m​2Fmm2 is the subgroup Ref. [124] inferred from the 11B shifts at 2.42.4 GPa, and for layer-alternating order no clear orthorhombic distortion is expected [5]) and couples linearly to shear strain along [110][110], whereas the empty-plaquette order parameter (A2A_{2}) couples linearly to no strain component. With the strain derivative of the spin gap, ∂Egap/∂ϵ≈700\partial E_{\rm gap}/\partial\epsilon\approx 700–900900 K from the longitudinal c11c_{11} mode [135], as the magnetoelastic scale, a shear strain above about 10−510^{-5} exceeds the full–empty splitting of the pure model, which is below 10−4​J′10^{-4}J^{\prime} [128], and near the critical pressure the strain is a uniform valence-bond field that outweighs the DM seed of Sec. X.3 by orders of magnitude at the band-touching scale. Random DM from the same local distortions scales as δ​D∼(D/J)​δ​J\delta D\sim(D/J)\,\delta J, so its covariance is smaller than that of δ​J\delta J by (D/J)2∼10−3(D/J)^{2}\sim 10^{-3}, and over the available RG time ln⁡(J′/T)≲7\ln(J^{\prime}/T)\lesssim 7 its marginal flow changes it by less than a percent; the sign of its one-loop coefficient below has no experimental consequence. The random VBS field is different. With a lattice-scale variance of order the defect density xx, it becomes strong near Tdis∼J′​x1/yΔT_{\rm dis}\sim J^{\prime}x^{1/y_{\Delta}}, which for yΔ=1.08y_{\Delta}=1.08 and x≈0.1x\approx 0.1–0.4%0.4\% is of order 0.10.1–0.30.3 K, comparable to T∗T^{*}, and exceeds it by more than an order of magnitude if the valence-bond dimension is as small as in bosonic-DQCP numerics [86]. The defects are magnetic. In an applied field their polarized polarons, imaged at ambient pressure for a cc-axis field in Ref. [132], are 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd random fields on the Néel channels for every field direction, because a local defect removes the lattice symmetry that forbids a uniform Néel moment for 𝑩|[001]\bm{B}\parallel[001]. The random-field protection of chirality and magnetism stated above therefore holds for the zero-field Hamiltonian and fails below any freezing of the orphan spins.

The static-randomness eigenvalues yΔ=2+2​z−2​ΔOy_{\Delta}=2+2z-2\Delta_{O} in two spatial dimensions then read as follows. A random VBS field has yΔ=4−2​ΔV=1.08y_{\Delta}=4-2\Delta_{V}=1.08 at leading order in 1/N1/N and is relevant. Current couplings have yΔ=0y_{\Delta}=0 at tree level, protected by conservation, and random velocities have yΔ=−2y_{\Delta}=-2. For the marginal set the one-loop variance flow of Appendix G, which contains the disordered-Dirac results of Ref. [72], gives the coefficients +2+2 (potential), −2-2 (mass) and 00 (abelian vector potential) in units of Δ2/(2​π)\Delta^{2}/(2\pi). For a smooth random modulation of the DM scale, δ​λ​(𝒓)​𝒪DM\delta\lambda(\bm{r})\,\mathcal{O}_{\rm DM}, the static vertex tensors vanish and the canonical normalization of the matrix-valued frequency renormalization gives

d​Δλd​ℓ=−2π​Δλ2,\frac{d\Delta_{\lambda}}{d\ell}=-\frac{2}{\pi}\Delta_{\lambda}^{2}, (27)

so this component is marginally irrelevant. DM randomness uncorrelated on the bond scale behaves differently. Matched on the π\pi-flux state, its covariance lies half in the spin-current sextet and half in the 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even staggered densities, with no 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd or mass component, and for independent Gaussian components on every bond the projected one-loop flow is

d​Δd​ℓ=+23​Δ22​π(+new directions),\frac{d\Delta}{d\ell}=+\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\Delta^{2}}{2\pi}\quad(+\text{new directions}), (28)

with an ensemble-dependent coefficient. Every bond-uncorrelated ensemble generates random 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even VBS masses, however, and these carry the relevant eigenvalue 1.081.08 at the SO(5) point, so bond-scale DM randomness adds to the random VBS field of δ​J\delta J instead of being inert. Its strength in the material is not derived.

Gauge fluctuations. With one SU(2) gauge field and one pair of Higgs triplets per replica, the covariance of the 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even random fields flows at O⁡(Δ2,Δ/N)O(\Delta^{2},\Delta/N) as

d​Δi​jd​ℓ=(4−Δi−Δj)​Δi​j+12​π​Bi​j​[Δ],\frac{d\Delta_{ij}}{d\ell}=(4-\Delta_{i}-\Delta_{j})\,\Delta_{ij}+\frac{1}{2\pi}\,B_{ij}[\Delta], (29)

where Δi\Delta_{i} is the O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) scaling dimension of the operator that carries the random field ii and BB is the NN-independent one-loop kernel of Appendix G. Gauge fluctuations enter only through Δi\Delta_{i}: the O⁡(Δ2)O(\Delta^{2}) graphs with one gauge propagator carry tr⁡σc=0\operatorname{tr}\sigma^{c}=0 (Fig. 6(h)), and those with two need a nonzero flavor trace, which no 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even singlet has. The VBS components keep ΔV=2−64​Cg/(3​π2​N)\Delta_{V}=2-64C_{g}/(3\pi^{2}N), so the random plaquette field has yΔ=128​Cg/(3​π2​N)=1.08y_{\Delta}=128C_{g}/(3\pi^{2}N)=1.08 at every value of the gauge parameter, and the conserved currents keep Δ=2\Delta=2, so current randomness is marginal at linear order to all orders in 1/N1/N. For the plaquette pair, with variances Δ+\Delta_{+} of the empty (A2A_{2}, μx+μz\mu^{x}+\mu^{z}) and Δ−\Delta_{-} of the full (B2B_{2}, μx−μz\mu^{x}-\mu^{z}) component and ΔJ\Delta_{J} of the VBS-rotation current γx,y​μy\gamma^{x,y}\mu^{y}, the flow closes:

d​Δ±d​ℓ\displaystyle\frac{d\Delta_{\pm}}{d\ell} =yΔΔ±+12​π[−2Δ±2+2Δ+Δ−\displaystyle=y_{\Delta}\Delta_{\pm}+\frac{1}{2\pi}\bigl[-2\Delta_{\pm}^{2}+2\Delta_{+}\Delta_{-}
∓4ΔJ(Δ+−Δ−)],\displaystyle\qquad\mp 4\Delta_{J}(\Delta_{+}-\Delta_{-})\bigr],
d​ΔJd​ℓ\displaystyle\frac{d\Delta_{J}}{d\ell} =Δ+​Δ−π.\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta_{+}\Delta_{-}}{\pi}. (30)

The one-loop terms cancel on S=Δ++Δ−S=\Delta_{+}+\Delta_{-}, which grows with the exponent yΔy_{\Delta}, while the full–empty imbalance δ​Δ=Δ+−Δ−\delta\Delta=\Delta_{+}-\Delta_{-} obeys d​δ​Δ/d​ℓ=[yΔ−(S+4​ΔJ)/π]​δ​Δd\,\delta\Delta/d\ell=[y_{\Delta}-(S+4\Delta_{J})/\pi]\,\delta\Delta and decays at strong disorder. The only fixed point with a single random plaquette component, Δ∗=π​yΔ\Delta^{*}=\pi y_{\Delta} with z∗=1+yΔ/2≃1.54z^{*}=1+y_{\Delta}/2\simeq 1.54, lies outside the weak-disorder regime and is unstable, with eigenvalue (1+3)​yΔ=2.95(1+\sqrt{3})\,y_{\Delta}=2.95 in the (Δ−,ΔJ)(\Delta_{-},\Delta_{J}) plane. Every 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even ensemble with a plaquette component therefore flows to strong disorder after a flow time of order yΔ−1​ln⁡(1/Δ0)y_{\Delta}^{-1}\ln(1/\Delta_{0}), which sets the scale TdisT_{\rm dis} used above. From 0.050.05 times the normalized covariance this takes ℓ∗=5.15\ell^{*}=5.15 for bond-uncorrelated interdimer exchange, 5.805.80 for vacancies and 9.69.6–10.610.6 for bond-uncorrelated DM randomness, whose trace without the gauge dressing grows only to 0.070.07–0.080.08 by ℓ=40\ell=40 (Appendix G).

Matched on the π\pi-flux state, bond-uncorrelated interdimer exchange disorder has the weights 1/41/4, 1/41/4 and 1/21/2 on Δ+\Delta_{+}, Δ−\Delta_{-} and ΔJ\Delta_{J}. Dimer-bond randomness has no zero-mode projection at mean-field order, but its site group allows it to feed Δ−\Delta_{-} beyond it. The two opposite interdimer bonds of a site project with opposite signs, so a spinless vacancy couples at mean-field order only through the imbalance δ​Jnear′−δ​Jfar′\delta J^{\prime}_{\rm near}-\delta J^{\prime}_{\rm far} between the modifications of the interdimer bonds on the side of its dimer partner and on the far side, with a variance of order x​(δ​Jnear′−δ​Jfar′)2/J′2x(\delta J^{\prime}_{\rm near}-\delta J^{\prime}_{\rm far})^{2}/J^{\prime 2} rather than xx. The mirror through the Cu site forbids the empty-plaquette component to all orders, so vacancies feed only the full plaquette and the VBS-rotation current, and the empty plaquette acquires its random field only through Eq. (30). The mean-field lattice with one site removed agrees (Appendix G). In the π\pi-flux parent the vacancy binds two quasi-localized zero modes that carry the freed spin 1/21/2 as a Kramers doublet, with neither magnetization nor chirality in its 𝒯\mathcal{T}-invariant average, and the induced bond-energy pattern is C4​vC_{4v} symmetric. In the Z3000 state the empty-plaquette harmonic vanishes after averaging over boundary twists, and the twist-averaged full plaquette and VBS-rotation current are (3CLOSE(3–OPEN10)×10−310)\times 10^{-3} of the bond energy per vacancy on clusters of 1212–2424 sites per side, the full plaquette extrapolating to (2CLOSE(2–OPEN6)×10−36)\times 10^{-3},, an order of magnitude below the isotropic harmonic that feeds random TcT_{c}. The zero modes correspond to the bound state of the earlier mean-field theories discussed in Ref. [64] for the staggered-flux state, where gauge fluctuations replace the free-spin Curie constant by a universal one and remove the staggered induced moment; that U(1) analysis is not carried over here to the SU(2) and Z3000 cases.

In large-NN noncompact QED3, time-reversal-invariant disorder that keeps a U(1)×\timesSU(NN) flavor symmetry, on the kagome lattice a random DM coupling along one spin axis, flows to a fixed line at finite disorder with continuously varying z>1z>1, whereas disorder that breaks the flavor symmetry further, including random-bond disorder through the valence-bond masses, flows to strong disorder, and random gauge flux becomes relevant beyond leading order [117]. Gauge screening stabilizes that theory against a weak random chemical potential, which couples to the U(1) gauge charge, while random Dirac masses drive it to a fixed point at finite disorder [32]. In that abelian limit the one-gauge-line graphs survive as parity-odd triangles, and Eq. (29) with them reproduces both results (Appendix G). In the SU(2) theory the triangles vanish, the chemical potential of the gauge charge is not a gauge-invariant coupling, and no conserved flux current exists at the multicritical point, so neither the fixed line nor the screening of a random chemical potential carries over. In compact QED3 with four flavors, time-reversal-invariant random spin currents, a non-abelian vector potential, lower the dimensions of monopoles of every charge [22]. This bears on the single allowed monopole of U800, already relevant in the large-NN extrapolation.

Chirality filter beyond N=∞N=\infty. Time reversal holds in every realization of non-magnetic disorder, so the replicated action is invariant under 𝒯\mathcal{T} acting on a single replica while the others are left unchanged. A replica-bilocal term ∫Oia​Ojb\int O_{i}^{a}O_{j}^{b} with a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd factor changes sign under this operation and is absent to all orders in Δ\Delta and 1/N1/N and for every cumulant of the disorder. The selection rule is stronger than invariance under a common 𝒯\mathcal{T} of all replicas, which would allow a variance Δ​Tr​[𝒳¯​𝒳]a​Tr​[𝒳¯​𝒳]b\Delta\,\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\mathcal{X}]_{a}\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\mathcal{X}]_{b}. The random-field protection of chirality and magnetism is therefore exact within the zero-field Hamiltonian, and gauge fluctuations change only the dimensions of the 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even channels. 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd operators enter the averaged theory only through 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even composites such as (Tr⁡[𝒳¯​𝒳])2(\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\mathcal{X}])^{2} in the SO(5)-singlet quartic channel, as random-TcT_{c} couplings of the chiral transition. Once 𝒯\mathcal{T} is broken, in a field or below the freezing of orphan spins, the Néel masses carry random fields with yΔ=1.08y_{\Delta}=1.08 and the flux mass a random field that is marginal at linear order to O⁡(1/N)O(1/N): its dimension 2+256​(Nf−Nb)/(π2​N2)2+256(N_{f}-N_{b})/(\pi^{2}N^{2}) equals 22 at Nf=Nb=2N_{f}=N_{b}=2, an accidental cancellation of the field content that no symmetry enforces.

Random TcT_{c}. The tuning parameter is represented by the constraint field σ\sigma of the Higgs sector. At O⁡(1/N)O(1/N)

Δσ=2−323​π2​M+64​Cs3​π2​N−64​W​Csπ2​N2,\Delta_{\sigma}=2-\frac{32}{3\pi^{2}M}+\frac{64C_{s}}{3\pi^{2}N}-\frac{64\,WC_{s}}{\pi^{2}N^{2}}, (31)

with M=6M=6 real Higgs components, the adjoint Casimir Cs=8C_{s}=8 in the normalization Cg=3C_{g}=3, and the Higgs loop weight W=8W=8. The three terms are the constraint-field exchange, one gauge line with its seagulls, and two gauge lines attached to a closed Higgs loop, the graphs of Fig. 8(a)–(c) (Appendix O); the constraint-field triangle gives no logarithm in d=3d=3, and the mixing with the flux singlet Tr⁡[𝒳¯​𝒳]\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\mathcal{X}], degenerate with σ\sigma at N=∞N=\infty, vanishes because the Higgs loop is parity even and the fermion loop parity odd, as time reversal requires. Every term is independent of the gauge parameter, and in the abelian limit Eq. (31) reproduces the correlation-length exponent of Ref. [58] [its Eq. (34)] for all NbN_{b} and NfN_{f}, including the CPN-1 value ν=1−48/(π2​N)\nu=1-48/(\pi^{2}N) [53, 120] at Nf=0N_{f}=0. At N=12N=12, Δσ=0.38\Delta_{\sigma}=0.38 lies below the unitarity bound 1/21/2 [80, 25], and the random-TcT_{c} eigenvalue is yTc=4−2​Δσ=3.24y_{T_{c}}=4-2\Delta_{\sigma}=3.24. Random TcT_{c} is therefore relevant at O⁡(1/N)O(1/N), and the Harris criterion fails at this order, but a correction of this size is not controlled at N=12N=12, and the O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) value of ν\nu carries no quantitative information there.

Higgs sector. The anisotropy bilinears Φ1⋅Φ1−Φ2⋅Φ2\Phi_{1}\cdot\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\cdot\Phi_{2} and Φ1⋅Φ2\Phi_{1}\cdot\Phi_{2} have Δ=1−64​Cs/(3​π2​N)+32/(3​π2​M)\Delta=1-64C_{s}/(3\pi^{2}N)+32/(3\pi^{2}M), whose gauge term, −1.44-1.44 at N=12N=12, is Cs/Cg=8/3C_{s}/C_{g}=8/3 times the fermion value and takes Δ\Delta below the unitarity bound. The expansion thus fixes only the direction: random Higgs anisotropies, with yΔ=2y_{\Delta}=2 at N=∞N=\infty, become more relevant. The gauge-invariant composites Φa​Tr​[σa​𝒳¯​M​𝒳]\Phi^{a}\mathrm{Tr}[\sigma^{a}\bar{\mathcal{X}}M\mathcal{X}], through which gauge-adjoint couplings can be random, have Δ=1.80\Delta=1.80 (mass type) and 1.621.62 (current type) at N=12N=12, against 5/25/2 at N=∞N=\infty (Appendix G), shifts that leave their relevance undecided. All of these operators are 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even where they carry random fields, so none of them affects the protection of chirality.

The consequences favor, but do not by themselves establish, an inversion of the clean-limit competition. The VBS channel condenses a discrete order parameter, the Ising plaquette pair of Sec. X.3, exposed to a relevant random field. Under strictly two-dimensional short-range random fields, the domain argument of Imry and Ma [51], marginal in two dimensions for discrete order and made rigorous by Aizenman and Wehr [2], at T>0T>0 for any field distribution in the ferromagnetic random-field Ising model and otherwise for continuously distributed disorder, with its quantum extension, including ground states, for continuously distributed disorder [36], shows that these fields destroy long-range VBS order for arbitrarily weak δ​J\delta J, leaving a plaquette domain glass with ξIM∼a​exp⁡[cIM​(JI/h)2]\xi_{\rm IM}\sim a\,\exp[c_{\rm IM}(J_{I}/h)^{2}], where hh is the rms random field per cell, JIJ_{I} the effective Ising coupling of the plaquette variables; the (JI/h)2(J_{I}/h)^{2} form is the T=0T=0 domain-breakup estimate of Ref. [4], with a constant of order unity, and exact ground states of the square-lattice random-field Ising model give cIM≃2.1±0.2c_{\rm IM}\simeq 2.1\pm 0.2 for Gaussian fields (1.9±0.21.9\pm 0.2 for bimodal ones) [99]. If each free spin pins its cell, h≃4​JI​4​xh\simeq 4J_{I}\sqrt{4x} for a free-spin fraction xx per Cu, and x=0.14%x=0.14\%, 0.4%0.4\% and 2.5%2.5\% give ξIM\xi_{\rm IM} of order e23​ae^{23}a, micrometers and a few cells; these estimates are exponentially sensitive to the assumed pinning strength. In three dimensions weak random fields do not destroy order [50, 7], and a layered crystal crosses over to that behavior once the interlayer coupling of the plaquette variables exceeds the random-field energy of a two-dimensional domain. For the full plaquette, whose order parameter couples linearly to strain, this coupling is elastic and three-dimensional, and smooth strain templates the domains instead of softening their formation. A plaquette domain glass is therefore expected in substituted crystals rather than in the nominally pure crystals studied so far, and a calorimetric anomaly does not decide between the two, since a 2D Ising peak that is sharp on the scale |T−TP|/TP∼0.1|T-T_{P}|/T_{P}\sim 0.1 probes correlation lengths of about ten cells. Random-singlet-like behavior does not follow from this: in Ref. [59] it requires spin-1/21/2 VBS defects, which a Lieb–Schultz–Mattis-type constraint enforces for half-odd-integer spin per unit cell, whereas the Shastry–Sutherland cell holds four spins 1/21/2 and the plaquette order is Ising-like, as for the two-leg ladder, where the unpaired spins at a domain wall form a singlet. Whether plaquette domain walls bind low-energy spins is not determined here. The chiral ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} channel sees at its thermal transition only random-TcT_{c}-type disorder, which is Harris-marginal for the 2D thermal Ising class [43, 123]. Weak bond disorder is in fact marginally irrelevant there, with logarithmic corrections [24, 102, 72]: the ln⁡ln\ln\ln specific heat of Ref. [24] is confirmed, while its spin-sector result, correlations decaying more slowly than any power, is contradicted by the exact bound of Ref. [102]. The ordered phase survives. The quantum transition with columnar-in-time disorder is a separate problem. Non-magnetic, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-invariant quenched disorder in zero field therefore supplies a chirality-filter mechanism, degrading the majority VBS channel while sparing the minority chiral one, in strictly two dimensions or at disorder strong enough that ξIM\xi_{\rm IM} falls below the interlayer length. Whether the system then orders chirally or remains a nonchiral glass depends on the sign and size of the residual chiral couplings. The random field destroys long-range VBS order but leaves local VBS gaps inside the domains, so the chiral channel gains no energetic advantage from it. Whether the filter makes thermal-Hall and weak-ferromagnetic signatures more likely in inhomogeneous samples is therefore a scenario that this analysis does not prove, and a sharp calorimetric anomaly does not mark a clean sample. Below T∗T^{*} the counting must be applied to projected vertices. Disorder with a nonzero zero-derivative projection on the QBT, the VBS random field foremost, has yΔ=2+2​z−2​ΔO=+2y_{\Delta}=2+2z-2\Delta_{O}=+2 and is strongly relevant, and a diffusive spinon regime preempting T∗⁣∗T^{**} becomes possible. Its stability against localization and gauge constraints is not settled here. Random λ\lambda itself projects to zero on the QBT, which is the null space of hDMh_{\rm DM} (Sec. X.1), so its leading projected coupling carries two derivatives and has yΔ=−2y_{\Delta}=-2. The scale-forming coupling is inert to its own randomness. At the pressure-tuned plaquette–antiferromagnet point, if the clean correlation-length exponent satisfies ν<1\nu<1, so that the two-dimensional Harris criterion 2​ν>22\nu>2 fails, random-TcT_{c} disorder is relevant [43, 13]. If the transition is instead weakly first order, quenched disorder rounds it in two dimensions [2, 49, 36]. The clean DQCP scaling should be rounded, while a distinct disordered critical point is not excluded, and rare-region (Griffiths) effects may accompany either outcome [123]. The finite-size-scaling correlation-length exponent of such a disordered critical point must obey νFS≥1\nu_{\rm FS}\geq 1 in two dimensions [13], a theorem for independent site or bond disorder given a suitable finite-size-scaling event. Existing high-pressure NMR does not report such rounding. Reference [20] attributes the satellite line broadening it observes at 2.12.1 GPa and 0.20.2 T to the lattice distortion of the full-plaquette state. It reports quantum-critical scaling of 1/T11/T_{1} between 0.20.2 and 22 K at 2.42.4 GPa, in near-cc fields just below the plaquette–antiferromagnet transition field. Reference [19], with 𝑩|c\bm{B}\parallel c at 2.42.4 GPa and 44 T, assigns its broad low-frequency 11B line to an empty-plaquette phase coexisting with the full-plaquette phase at a first-order, pressure-driven transition.

XIII Experimental signatures

Table 7 collects the predictions by probe.

XIII.1 Units, couplings, and scales

We use J=85J=85 K and J′=54J^{\prime}=54 K [84, 10]; the other parameter sets are listed in Sec. II. The spinon hopping t≃0.4​J′≃20t\simeq 0.4J^{\prime}\simeq 20–2222 K for J′=51J^{\prime}=51–5454 K (J′/J=0.60J^{\prime}/J=0.60–0.6350.635 at J=85J=85 K) is a mean-field estimate fixed by no measurement. It enters T∗T^{*} through the node splitting and the second-order scales through D⟂′/tD^{\prime}_{\perp}/t, whereas the length ξDM\xi_{\rm DM} does not depend on it (Sec. IX.1).

The DM couplings and their extraction are given in Sec. II: D⟂′≃0.09D^{\prime}_{\perp}\simeq 0.09–0.180.18 meV, the only intralayer DM coupling above TsT_{s}; the intra-dimer D≃0.22D\simeq 0.22–0.350.35 meV, the largest; the spectroscopic combination D~∥≃0.07\tilde{D}_{\parallel}\simeq 0.07–0.080.08 meV; and DΣ′≃−0.014D^{\prime}_{\Sigma}\simeq-0.014 meV from Table II of Ref. [77]. The in-plane components require the buckling, which persists down to 22 K at ambient pressure [121]; under pressure the cell stays tetragonal up to the monoclinic onset at 4.04.0–5.05.0 GPa [71, 134], near 44 GPa at low temperature [127], but no refinement determines the buckling there, and Ref. [71] suggests that it decreases. The crystals are inversion twins, which carry opposite in-plane DM; the magnetization, κx​y\kappa_{xy}, the NMR spectra and the plaquette selector b2b_{2}, which is even in λ\lambda, are twin-insensitive. All lattice energies quoted in units of tt or in kelvin are physical excitation energies, in the convention of Appendix A.

The scales of the theory are ranges. The crossover energy is T∗≃0.03T^{*}\simeq 0.03–0.170.17 K (Sec. IX.1). The thermodynamic crossover of the free-spinon specific heat lies near (0.1CLOSE(0.1–OPEN0.15)​T∗0.15)\,T^{*}, i.e. at 33–2525 mK. The associated length is ξDM=2​(J′/|DΣ′|)​a≃250\xi_{\rm DM}=\sqrt{2}\,(J^{\prime}/|D^{\prime}_{\Sigma}|)\,a\simeq 250–940940 lattice spacings. The lower edge of the quadratic-band-touching window is the Higgs-induced splitting δ′=(cΦ​sH​t)2/4​λ\delta^{\prime}=(c_{\Phi}s_{H}t)^{2}/4\lambda with cΦ≃0.67c_{\Phi}\simeq 0.67, Eq. (18), where the Higgs deviation sHs_{H} is fixed by no measurement. The flow applies on [δ′,λ][\delta^{\prime},\lambda], where the band touching screens the gauge field into a color-density interaction (Sec. X.1). That interaction diverges at ℓ∗≃0.6\ell^{*}\simeq 0.6–1.61.6, so the window requires ln⁡[2​λ/(cΦ​sH​t)]≳ℓ∗\ln[2\lambda/(c_{\Phi}s_{H}t)]\gtrsim\ell^{*}, i.e. cΦ​sH​t≲0.5​λc_{\Phi}s_{H}t\lesssim 0.5\lambda. It is open only near the critical pressure and closed deep in the Higgsed phase. Within it the instability temperature is T∗⁣∗≃(0.03CLOSET^{**}\simeq(0.03–OPEN0.1)​λ0.1)\lambda, or at the Fock level 0.20.2–2.52.5 mK (up to 44 mK with t≃0.4​J′t\simeq 0.4J^{\prime}), an order-of-magnitude one-loop estimate at order-one coupling.

XIII.2 Signatures by probe

XIII.2.1 Specific heat

Above T∗T^{*} the Dirac spin liquid and the pseudocritical regime survive with DM corrections controlled by T∗/TT^{*}/T, and at linear order in the DM couplings the specific heat carries no DM-induced feature; the second-order anisotropy of Sec. VIII, if the rank-2 SO(5) tensor is relevant, would instead produce a symmetry-breaking crossover at a scale of order T∗T^{*} or above. Below T∗T^{*} and near the critical pressure the Dirac cones reconstruct into the quadratic band touching of Sec. IX.2, which has a finite spinon density of states at mean field. The resulting C∝TC\propto T appears only well below the thermodynamic crossover near (0.1CLOSE(0.1–OPEN0.15)​T∗0.15)\,T^{*}, i.e. in the millikelvin range, and only if T∗⁣∗≲0.1​λT^{**}\lesssim 0.1\lambda (Sec. IX.1). We quote no coefficient for this term, which requires the QBT curvature beyond mean field, and we do not compute the thermodynamic signature of the crossover itself. All existing zero-field data near the plaquette–antiferromagnet boundary lie above T∗T^{*}. The a.c. calorimetry of Ref. [39] reaches 0.40.4 K and locates a first-order boundary at 2.782.78 GPa ending in a bicritical point. That work fits C/T=a0+a1T2+(a2/T3)e−Δ/TC/T=a_{0}+a_{1}T^{2}+(a_{2}/T^{3})\,e^{-\Delta/T} and concludes that a clean system is gapless above 2.72.7 GPa. Its lowest-temperature C/TC/T, roughly a0a_{0}, is enhanced around the critical pressure of 2.782.78 GPa, which the authors tentatively attribute to enhanced fluctuations near the bicritical point. These data lie at least a factor of two above T∗T^{*} (four at the Fock level). They lie inside the plaquette and Néel phases, whose ordering temperatures exceed 11 K, so the enhancement does not test the spinon density of states of Sec. IX.2. The calorimetry of Ref. [67] reaches 0.10.1 K, and its zero-field data cover 00–26.526.5 kbar. That work expects the peak near 22 K, seen for P≥18P\geq 18 kbar up to its highest pressure, to mark the thermal transition out of the gapped plaquette phase. On its own pressure scale its data below that peak therefore lie in the plaquette phase. Its lowest temperatures lie within the range of T∗T^{*}, still inside that phase.

In applied fields Ref. [40] finds, at fields where the zero-field order (plaquette at 2.682.68 and 2.752.75 GPa, antiferromagnetic at 2.92.9 GPa) is suppressed and the field-induced antiferromagnet has not set in, a specific heat linear in TT from about 11–1.71.7 K down to 0.40.4 K, over 1.51.5–44 T at 2.682.68 GPa, 33–77 T at 2.752.75 GPa and 2.52.5–44 T at 2.92.9 GPa, with intercepts quoted as C/T≃1.1C/T\simeq 1.1–1.41.4, 1.11.1–1.61.6 and 1.21.2 J K-2 mol-1 at the three pressures, and reproduced on a second sample at 2.922.92 GPa. It regards fractionalized spin excitations as one possible origin and leaves the mechanism open. A thermal tensor-network study of the SS model in a Zeeman field, on 3×12×43\times 12\times 4-site cylinders, finds a TT-linear specific heat at intermediate fields inside the plaquette phase and near its boundary with the antiferromagnet, within the reach of its system size and bond dimension [109]; that model has full spin-rotation symmetry, so the field direction does not enter there, whereas with DM it does. In Ref. [40] the field was applied essentially along the cc axis, and C/TC/T is quoted per mole of formula units [37]. At mean field a Zeeman field splits the Dirac cones into spinon Fermi pockets, which for 𝑩|c\bm{B}\parallel c the DM couplings gap at about 0.4×4​λ0.4\times 4\lambda (Sec. XI). For 0.4×4​λ≪kB​T≪g​μB​B/20.4\times 4\lambda\ll k_{B}T\ll g\mu_{B}B/2 their density of states, and hence C/TC/T, grows linearly with BB. With t≃20t\simeq 20 K its value at 44 T is about 0.070.07 J K-2 per mole of formula units (0.160.16 with the Fock hopping), seven to twenty-three times below the reported intercepts, so the free-spinon pockets do not account for them. The field also activates different masses for different orientations (Sec. XI): the chirality mass alone for 𝑩|c\bm{B}\parallel c, and the Néel components for an in-plane field, each requiring at least first order in spin–orbit coupling. The TT-linear data, taken with 𝑩|c\bm{B}\parallel c, probe the orientation that activates only the chirality mass; a measurement with 𝑩|[100]\bm{B}\parallel[100] in the same regime would test the selection rule where the spinon density of states is largest. These data lie above T∗T^{*}.

XIII.2.2 NMR

The classification of Sec. XI gives an orientation-selective Néel response. For 𝑩|[100]\bm{B}\parallel[100] a staggered (Néel) moment perpendicular to 𝑩\bm{B} is activated at linear order in BB. It is of second order in the in-plane DM couplings, λD′∥,s\lambda D^{\prime}_{\parallel,s} at mean field, and of first order in a dimer-dependent in-plane gg anisotropy. Its singular part scales as ξ3−2​ΔN\xi^{3-2\Delta_{N}} with 3−2​ΔN=+0.083-2\Delta_{N}=+0.08 at leading order in 1/N1/N, a weak enhancement that becomes strong for the smaller ΔN\Delta_{N} of bosonic-DQCP numerics [86]. For 𝑩|[001]\bm{B}\parallel[001] no Néel moment is allowed and the flux channel is the only activated mass. Intra-dimer staggered moments of the type of Ref. [63] are not excluded. For 𝑩|[110]\bm{B}\parallel[110] the Néel component along 𝑩\bm{B}, (Nx+Ny)/2(N^{x}+N^{y})/\sqrt{2}, appears linearly in BB and a valence-bond imbalance Vx−VyV_{x}-V_{y} appears at order Bx​ByB_{x}B_{y}, second order in the DM couplings. The magnitude of the moment in μB\mu_{B}, which requires a matrix-element calculation, and the spin-lattice rate 1/T11/T_{1} are not computed. The proposed test is 11B NMR at 2.42.4–2.82.8 GPa comparing 𝑩|[100]\bm{B}\parallel[100] with 𝑩|[001]\bm{B}\parallel[001] at matched g​μB​Bg\mu_{B}B. The matching uses ga=2.05g_{a}=2.05 and gc=2.28g_{c}=2.28, which Ref. [87] obtained by ESR at ambient pressure from the paramagnetic resonance at 2525 K, and it assumes that pressure changes these values little. The comparison should be made below the field-induced transition, which lies at 5.55.5–5.75.7 T at 2.42.4 GPa for a field along or near cc [20, 19]. It should also be made above the plaquette ordering temperature, TP=1.6T_{P}=1.6 K at 2.42.4 GPa in a cc-axis field of 44 T [19]. If the plaquette phase lowers the tetragonal symmetry, it allows additional DM components that are not classified here (Sec. XIV). The induced staggered field is even under the sign reversal of the in-plane DM components between inversion twins, so the induced moment has the same sign in both twin domains. No existing experiment makes this comparison. Reference [124] compared 𝑩|c\bm{B}\parallel c with 𝑩|[110]\bm{B}\parallel[110] at 2.42.4 GPa and 77 T down to 2.12.1 K and found, for 𝑩|c\bm{B}\parallel c below 3030 K, a loss of fourfold symmetry in the magnetic shifts; no [100][100] data exist. Reference [20] measured at pressures up to 2.42.4 GPa, in 0.20.2–1515 T and down to 0.070.07 K, with the field 8.6∘8.6^{\circ} from cc. Its in-plane component, about 0.15​B0.15B, points along an in-plane direction that was not characterized. Reference [19] used 𝑩|c\bm{B}\parallel c to 2.652.65 GPa between 0.30.3 and 55 K. Reference [127] applied all fields in the a​bab plane and made no orientation comparison. At 2.42.4 GPa it has spectra for 𝑩|a\bm{B}\parallel a at 88 T down to 1.81.8 K, and they show no line splitting on cooling. These temperatures lie above the Néel temperature found at 2.42.4 GPa for 𝑩|c\bm{B}\parallel c, which increases monotonically with field to 1.51.5 K at 1010 T [19]. The 𝑩|a+b\bm{B}\parallel a{+}b spectra of Ref. [127] are at 44–1414 GPa, and its other in-plane data, at 11–88 T, span 2.652.65–1414 GPa. Above the monoclinic onset at 4.04.0–5.05.0 GPa [134] these data probe a lower lattice symmetry than the one classified here. The antiferromagnet above Hc≃5.7H_{c}\simeq 5.7–6.26.2 T with moments along aa or bb [20] is the thermodynamic field-induced phase and is distinct from the DM-activated mass.

XIII.2.3 Thermal Hall effect and magnetization

The chiral minority phase of Sec. X.2 has CBdG=∓4C_{\rm BdG}=\mp 4 and c=∓2c=\mp 2, hence a quantized κx​y/T→∓2π2kB2/3h≃∓1.9×10−12\kappa_{xy}/T\to\mp 2\pi^{2}k_{B}^{2}/3h\simeq\mp 1.9\times 10^{-12} W K-2 per layer as T→0T\to 0, conditional on a gapped deconfined ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} sector. With two CuBO3 layers per cc-axis lattice constant of 6.6496.649 Å, from single-crystal x-ray diffraction at ambient conditions [108, 54] (6.6416.641 Å at 22 K [121]), the bulk value is κx​y/T≃∓5.7×10−3\kappa_{xy}/T\simeq\mp 5.7\times 10^{-3} W K-2 m-1, that is, |κx​y|≃6|\kappa_{xy}|\simeq 6 μ\muW K-1 m-1 at 11 mK, the scale of T∗⁣∗T^{**}, if the plateau is reached there. The cc axis shortens under pressure, by about 6%6\% at 5.55.5 GPa [28], so the bulk value in the pressurized chiral liquid is slightly larger. A weak uniform magnetization MzM_{z} accompanies the chirality. Its magnitude is not computed, and at mean field its sign satisfies Mz​κx​y>0M_{z}\kappa_{xy}>0 for the magnetic moment MzM_{z} and 𝑱Q=−κ∇T\bm{J}^{Q}=-\kappa\nabla T (Appendix J). A cc-axis field couples linearly to the flux channel, because MzM_{z} and the flux mass carry the same one-dimensional representation of the buckled and of the high-temperature spin–orbit-locked groups. Without spin–orbit coupling they do not. The twin operation leaves both invariant, so the two twin domains respond alike. Cooling through T∗⁣∗T^{**} in 𝑩|[001]\bm{B}\parallel[001] therefore selects the chirality domain whose moment is parallel to the field. For the Zeeman coupling gc​μB​𝑩⋅𝑺g_{c}\mu_{B}\bm{B}\cdot\bm{S} of Cu2+ that domain has κx​y​Bc>0\kappa_{xy}B_{c}>0 at mean field, with BcB_{c} the field component along +c+c. On the QBT the Zeeman term is itself the flux mass (Sec. XI). Below T∗T^{*} the field therefore also opens the flux gap without spontaneous order, with lowest excitation energy gc​μB​B/2g_{c}\mu_{B}B/2 at weak field, and at mean field this field-only state has the Chern number of the domain the field selects. A thermal Hall signal measured in the field, including a plateau, therefore does not distinguish the chiral phase from the field-gapped QBT. The test of spontaneous chirality is the remanent κx​y\kappa_{xy} at zero field after field cooling. It has the sign of κx​y\kappa_{xy} in the cooling field, reverses with that field, and comes with hysteresis of κx​y​(B)\kappa_{xy}(B) and Mz​(B)M_{z}(B) below T∗⁣∗T^{**} that disappears above T∗⁣∗T^{**}. The cooling field must keep the field-induced gap gc​μB​B/2g_{c}\mu_{B}B/2 below kB​T∗⁣∗k_{B}T^{**}, so that it selects a domain and does not decide the phase. For T∗⁣∗≃0.2T^{**}\simeq 0.2–2.52.5 mK this requires B≲0.07B\lesssim 0.07–0.80.8 mT (gc​μB​B/2​kB≃0.05g_{c}\mu_{B}B/2k_{B}\simeq 0.05–0.60.6 mK). The field needed to select a single domain depends on the magnitude of MzM_{z} and is not computed. The ambient-pressure thermal Hall measurements of Refs. [90, 113], both with 𝑩|c\bm{B}\parallel c and the heat current along aa, resolved no κx​y\kappa_{xy}. Reference [90] reports no signal of the predicted triplon magnitude at 7.57.5 and 1010 K in fields up to 33 T. Reference [113] bounds |κx​y||\kappa_{xy}| at 77, 8.58.5, and 1010 K by 2020–30%30\% of its own non-interacting-triplon calculation. That calculation is opposite in sign to, and smaller by a factor 2​π2\pi than, those of Refs. [79, 94]. These nulls constrain the triplon mechanism of the dimer phase and leave the pressurized chiral liquid untested, since no thermal Hall measurement under pressure exists. Reference [20] infers the uniform magnetization from the 11B Knight shift at 2.12.1 GPa and 0.070.07 K in a near-cc field. The magnetization stays below 2%2\% of the saturated moment from 55 to 1515 T, and at 1515 T the system is inside the field-induced antiferromagnet. The zero-field MzM_{z} below T∗⁣∗T^{**} is therefore untested.

XIII.2.4 Neutron, Raman, and ESR spectroscopy

Below T∗T^{*} the only gauge-singlet gap channels of the reconstructed spectrum are the two valence-bond components and the scalar chirality, and no Néel gap channel exists, a kinematic statement. The node reconstruction takes place at the energy 4​λ≃T∗4\lambda\simeq T^{*}, that is, 0.0030.003–0.0150.015 meV. We do not compute the dynamic structure factor, the Raman response, or the ESR spectrum. The D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp}-dominated one-triplon splitting of 8585 GHz [88, 10, 30] and the triplon Chern bands [94, 79] are quantities of the dimer phase and do not test the present theory.

XIII.2.5 Plaquette phase type versus pressure

Within the VBS doublet, and near the critical pressure, the order parameter is a two-state Ising pair (Sec. X.3). Below T∗T^{*} the DM-induced correction to the selection that the pure Shastry–Sutherland model makes is a bias of at most of order 10−410^{-4} after the running to the band-touching scale. Which of its two contributions leads, a seed linear in D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp}, which favors the full-plaquette pair for D⟂′<0D^{\prime}_{\perp}<0, or the determinant term, which favors the empty one, depends on the Higgs sector of the SO(5)-singlet channel, which is not controlled at N=12N=12, so the direction is not established (Sec. X.3). The pure-model selection itself is not computed here. The iPEPS study of Ref. [17] and the infinite density-matrix renormalization-group study of Ref. [68] find the empty (square) plaquette state, and Ref. [68] chooses the sign λ2>0\lambda_{2}>0 of its monopole anisotropy to match it. The high-pressure 11B NMR of Ref. [19], a preprint, resolves two plaquette phases that coexist across a first-order pressure-driven transition. The empty-plaquette fraction rises to 70%70\% at 2.652.65 GPa, and the empty-plaquette phase borders the antiferromagnet. The same work reports, at 2.42.4 GPa with 𝑩|c\bm{B}\parallel c, a field-induced transition from the empty-plaquette phase to the antiferromagnet near 5.55.5 T, with 1/T1∝T0.61/T_{1}\propto T^{0.6} between 0.30.3 and 1.51.5 K at 5.55.5 T. It also reports a plaquette ordering at TP=1.6T_{P}=1.6 K at 2.42.4 GPa and 44 T, which the authors assign to the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} (Ising) breaking of the twofold degeneracy shared by both plaquette phases. The Ising thermal transition near 22 K in zero field is seen in calorimetry [67, 38]. The empty and full labels of Ref. [19] rest on an interpretation of NMR lineshapes and relaxation. Other work favors the full-plaquette phase at similar pressures. The neutron intensities of Ref. [133] at 2.152.15 GPa tentatively favor it, and Ref. [20] attributes an NMR satellite broadening at 2.12.1 GPa and 0.20.2 T to a full-plaquette lattice distortion. Reference [105] interprets two high-field phases, measured with 𝑩\bm{B} in the a​bab plane, as full-plaquette descendants, although its iPEPS calculations also find both phases in the undeformed model, whose low-field phase is the empty plaquette. The deformed-coupling calculation of Ref. [5] reaches the same conclusion by comparison with the neutron data of Ref. [133] and with NMR, ESR and specific-heat data, so it is not independent of them. Reference [67] also expects the state it observes above 1.81.8 GPa and below 22 K to be the full-plaquette phase. In the model itself the empty plaquette remains the ground state, but near the upper edge of the plaquette phase (J′/J≈0.79J^{\prime}/J\approx 0.79) the full plaquette lies less than 10−4​J′10^{-4}J^{\prime} above it [128]. In the gapped plaquette phases a correction odd in D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} is at least of order D⟂′​D∥2D^{\prime}_{\perp}D_{\parallel}^{2} (Sec. X.3), and the band-touching seed linear in D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} exists only below T∗T^{*}, far below the plaquette ordering temperature, so DM does not decide between the two plaquette phases at TPT_{P}. Shear strain, to which the full-plaquette order parameter couples linearly and the empty one does not (Sec. XII), is the more likely selector at that scale. The present theory speaks only to the phase adjacent to the critical point, and it does not compute the plaquette transition temperature or its order.

XIII.2.6 Disorder

Section XII predicts, for strictly two-dimensional random fields or for substituted crystals, a plaquette domain glass, with chirality random-field protected for 𝒯\mathcal{T}-invariant disorder in zero field to all orders in the disorder and in 1/N1/N, random TcT_{c} relevant at O⁡(1/N)O(1/N), a full-plaquette order parameter that couples linearly to shear strain along [110][110] while the empty one does not, and vacancies that feed only the full-plaquette component of the random field. Several high-pressure studies invoke pressure inhomogeneity. Reference [20] suggests that it may cause the 11B NMR line splittings reported at 2.42.4 GPa and 77 T in Ref. [124], whose authors ascribed them instead to an intrinsic magnetic origin and a novel ordered phase. Reference [19] notes that neutron scattering just above the dimer–plaquette boundary favored the full-plaquette phase [133], while zero-field specific-heat data [67, 39] align with its own NMR data for the plaquette-liquid regime above the empty-plaquette phase. It names the degree of hydrostaticity achieved in each experiment as one possible source of this discrepancy. It also offers a more homogeneous high-pressure phase as one possible interpretation of its Néel temperatures of the field-induced antiferromagnet at 2.42.4 GPa, which are over 50%50\% higher than those of Ref. [20]. Reference [39] attributes the narrow overlap of its plaquette and antiferromagnetic phases to a tiny inhomogeneity of the pressure. Zero-field calorimetry in pressure cells loaded with liquid media resolves a specific-heat peak at the plaquette ordering temperature, at T≲2T\lesssim 2 K [67, 38, 39]. References [67, 38] interpret it as a thermal Ising (ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}) transition out of the plaquette phase, and Ref. [39] does not discuss its universality class. These peaks are consistent with the clean-sample expectation but do not discriminate it from weak disorder. The one controlled-disorder experiment under pressure, magnetometry on SrCu2-xMgx(BO3)2 with x≤0.05x\leq 0.05 at 2.12.1–2.42.4 GPa, suggests that the dopants destabilize the plaquette phase in favor of the antiferromagnet [105]. Neither it nor any other experiment tests the domain-glass or chirality-filter statements, and the strength and correlation structure of the material’s DM randomness are not known. The symmetry analysis of Sec. XII suggests four tests. (1) Because shear strain along [110][110] couples linearly to the full-plaquette order parameter and not to the empty one, the full-plaquette fraction resolved by NMR [19] should grow with the non-hydrostatic stress of the pressure environment and depend on the loading history; a uniaxial stress of 0.010.01–0.10.1 GPa along [110][110] should convert empty into full plaquettes and select one full-plaquette domain, while stress along [100][100] couples linearly to neither and serves as a control. (2) A full-plaquette order that is the same in all layers carries an orthorhombic strain, estimated at 10−410^{-4}–10−310^{-3}, that splits the (h​h​0)(hh0) reflections in high-resolution diffraction under helium pressure below TPT_{P}; the peak widths then measure the domain size. (3) Substituted crystals across the critical pressure should show a broadened or absent 22 K plaquette anomaly and, if the freed spins form a random-singlet-like network, the scaling collapse C/T∼H−γ​Fq​(T/H)C/T\sim H^{-\gamma}F_{q}(T/H) of Ref. [60], with γ\gamma the exponent of the zero-field C∼T1−γC\sim T^{1-\gamma} and χ∼T−γ\chi\sim T^{-\gamma} and an integer q∈{0,1,2}q\in\{0,1,2\} set by how spatial symmetries constrain the DM couplings; random-singlet states also arise from bond disorder in a ℤ4\mathbb{Z}_{4} columnar valence-bond solid, with spinons where four domain walls meet, whereas site dilution of the same model gives antiferromagnetic order [69]. (4) Tests of the physics below T∗T^{*} require free-spin fractions below about 10−310^{-3}, residual shear strain below about 10−510^{-5}, and a subtraction of the orphan-spin contribution, whose entropy x​R​ln⁡2xR\ln 2 is released near their mutual coupling scale. The comparison of [100][100] and [001][001] fields in NMR must separate a uniform line splitting from the polaron satellites that defects produce [132], and muon-spin relaxation is not a clean probe of 𝒯\mathcal{T} breaking here, since muons on the Cu–O–Cu path appear to break the dimer singlet locally [1].

XIII.3 Status of the predictions and decisive tests

Crossover scale. The prediction is a node reconstruction at T∗≃0.03T^{*}\simeq 0.03–0.170.17 K near the critical pressure, with a thermodynamic crossover to the QBT regime near (0.1CLOSE(0.1–OPEN0.15)​T∗0.15)\,T^{*}. All existing low-temperature data lie above or near T∗T^{*}. The NMR data of Refs. [20, 19] that come closest are taken in near-cc fields of several tesla. Near the field-induced transition at 2.42.4 GPa, Ref. [19] reports 1/T1∝T0.61/T_{1}\propto T^{0.6} from 0.30.3 to 1.51.5 K at 5.55.5 T along cc. At the same pressure, with the field 8.6∘8.6^{\circ} from cc, Ref. [20] fits the shifted rate 1/T1+bH∝T0.21/T_{1}+b_{H}\propto T^{0.2}, with a field-dependent offset bHb_{H}, for several fields close to Hc≃5.72H_{c}\simeq 5.72 T. Each fit holds only above a field-dependent onset TPT_{P}, below which the rate is thermally activated, and the fits together span 0.20.2 to 22 K. At 5.45.4–5.65.6 T this onset, which Ref. [20] identifies with the plaquette transition, lies between about 0.40.4 and 0.70.7 K. A cc-axis field couples only to the flux channel, and the in-plane component of about 0.15​B0.15B in Ref. [20] also activates a Néel channel (Table 6). The theory makes no statement about 1/T11/T_{1} in either case. The crossover is untested. A test requires measurements below about 0.10.1 K near the critical pressure in samples that remain disordered there, and the free-spinon C∝TC\propto T requires millikelvin temperatures.

Stability of criticality above T∗T^{*}. The absence of gauge-singlet masses and the irrelevance of D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} imply that DM cannot cause a departure from criticality above T∗T^{*} at linear order. The second-order anisotropies of Sec. VIII act there only if the rank-2 SO(5) tensor is relevant; their SO(3)×\timesSO(2)-invariant part has the form of the Néel–VBS tuning operator [118, 125, 137] and only shifts the critical pressure, so the candidate is the easy-axis or easy-plane spin anisotropy, at a scale of order T∗T^{*} or above, up to about 11 K. The DM-induced Yukawa couplings stay below the Yukawa coupling that bounds the pseudocritical window (Sec. VI). Reference [39] reports zero-field transitions into the plaquette and antiferromagnetic phases at about 1.21.2–1.61.6 K at 2.62.6–2.92.9 GPa, extrapolated to a bicritical point at 2.782.78 GPa near 1.31.3 K, and infers a first-order transition from the abrupt change of phase and from the drop of the fitted activation gap. These transitions and the gap fits, down to 0.40.4 K, lie above T∗T^{*}. In the field-tuned NMR of Ref. [20] the plaquette–antiferromagnet transition is first order at 2.12.1 and 2.42.4 GPa, with a discontinuity that weakens with pressure, and 1/T11/T_{1} shows critical scaling only at 2.42.4 GPa; Ref. [19] finds the field-induced transition out of the phase it assigns as empty plaquette continuous or nearly so. Apart from a relevant rank-2 tensor, the present theory attributes departures from continuous criticality to the interlayer coupling Jc≃0.6J_{c}\simeq 0.6 K, to disorder, to the multicritical character of the SO(5) point once a singlet is relevant, or to an intrinsically weakly first-order transition, as iPEPS finds at the plaquette boundary of the pure model [18]. The finite-temperature iPEPS calculations of Ref. [67], with an intra-dimer DM coupling of the size known for the material (D/J≃0.03D/J\simeq 0.03), show no qualitative effect on the dimer–plaquette critical point, which the same work locates experimentally at Pc≈19P_{c}\approx 19 kbar and Tc≈3.3T_{c}\approx 3.3 K. The spin-wave analysis of Ref. [28] attributes the 1.90​(8)1.90(8) meV excitation at (0,1,0)(0,1,0) of the antiferromagnet at 5.55.5 GPa to the interlayer coupling Jc=0.053​(3)J_{c}=0.053(3) meV, since a two-dimensional model would need an intra-dimer DM coupling of about 0.7​J′0.7J^{\prime}, close to 33 meV for its fitted J′=4.28J^{\prime}=4.28 meV, and D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} opens no gap there; inelastic neutron data at 4.24.2 GPa favor the same interlayer model [8]. These data lie at or above the monoclinic onset [134], and neither they nor the iPEPS calculation, which omits D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp}, tests the inertness of D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp}, which dominates only the triplon spectrum of the dimer phase.

Plaquette type. The DM correction is a small bias below T∗T^{*} whose direction the theory does not fix: the seed linear in D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} favors, for the NMR sign D⟂′<0D^{\prime}_{\perp}<0, the full plaquette, the pattern of the interpretations of Refs. [133, 105, 5] summarized in Sec. XIII.2, and the lattice determinant favors the empty plaquette of Ref. [19] adjacent to the antiferromagnet; the pure-model selection outweighs both at TPT_{P}. In Ref. [5] the full-plaquette phase is an instability of the coupled spin–lattice system, stabilized by inequivalent intra- or inter-dimer couplings, and a direct transition into it from the dimer phase would have to occur below J′/J=0.675J^{\prime}/J=0.675, where the Shastry–Sutherland model enters the empty-plaquette phase; the plaquette type thus indicates which parent state controls each pressure window. The full-plaquette evidence of Refs. [133, 105] comes from pressures of at most 2.42.4 GPa. Reference [19] finds the full-plaquette phase coexisting with the empty-plaquette phase from 1.851.85 GPa up to its highest pressure of 2.652.65 GPa. The decisive tests are an independent determination of the sign of D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp}, a bound on the SO(5)-singlet spectrum, and a zero-field structural or spectroscopic identification of the plaquette pattern adjacent to the antiferromagnet. The Ising order-parameter symmetry does not discriminate, since both plaquette phases are twofold degenerate [67, 19].

Chiral minority phase. The chiral phase is untested. The decisive test is a thermal Hall measurement under pressure in zero field below T∗⁣∗T^{**}, which lies below T∗≃0.03T^{*}\simeq 0.03–0.170.17 K, after cooling in a weak cc-axis field of 0.070.07–0.80.8 mT, chosen so that gc​μB​B/2≲kB​T∗⁣∗g_{c}\mu_{B}B/2\lesssim k_{B}T^{**} (Sec. XIII.2). The remanent κx​y/T\kappa_{xy}/T is compared with the plateau value given there. Its sign must follow the sign of the cooling field, and κx​y​(B)\kappa_{xy}(B) must be hysteretic below T∗⁣∗T^{**} only. A weak remanent MzM_{z} parallel to the cooling field completes the test.

Field orientation. The [100][100] versus [001][001] Néel response and the [110][110] valence-bond imbalance are untested; the test is the matched-field NMR comparison of Sec. XIII.2.

Disorder. The resolved calorimetric plaquette peaks are consistent with the clean-sample prediction, but the chirality filter is untested as such. The decisive test is a controlled-disorder study under pressure, for example calorimetry and NMR on the same crystal in media of different hydrostaticity, or Mg-substituted crystals [105, 21] across the critical pressure. At ambient pressure Mg substitution keeps the spin gap open, although the effective gap of powders falls from 2626 to 20.520.5 K at nominal x=0.05x=0.05 [107], and muon-spin relaxation on powders with up to 6%6\% nominal Mg finds no doping-induced static order, only a quasi-static component below 3.753.75 K that is present already at x=0x=0 [66]. Each substituted Cu frees a spin 1/21/2 on its dimer partner [41, 106], so the substitution adds magnetic polarons rather than spinless vacancies, and it tests the random-field statements only in zero field and above the freezing of those moments.

XIV Scope and limitations

The following items are not computed in this paper or are computed only at the stated level.

  • •

    The 1/N1/N expansion parameter 64/(π2​N)64/(\pi^{2}N) is 0.540.54 at N=12N=12, so the leading-order numbers ΔV=1.46\Delta_{V}=1.46, γ2adj=0.324\gamma_{2}^{\rm adj}=0.324, the lifting Δflux−ΔVBS=0.54\Delta_{\rm flux}-\Delta_{\rm VBS}=0.54, and yΔ=1.08y_{\Delta}=1.08 are qualitative and fix only signs and orderings. The abelian next-to-leading-order analogue, 0.217/N=1.8%0.217/N=1.8\%, applies to the abelian problem only, and no controlled next-order result exists for the mixed gauge–Higgs theory.

  • •

    The prefactor of T∗T^{*} is mean field, uncertain by a factor of order one (the Fock value and the twist of the assumed hopping t≃0.4​J′t\simeq 0.4J^{\prime} differ by a factor 1.71.7). DΣ′D^{\prime}_{\Sigma} rests on one DFT calculation [77], whose tabulated vectors are covariant under the crystal symmetry only pair by pair; the bond-axis component (0.010.01 meV) is the same on all four bonds, at the limit of its precision, and vanishes in the arXiv version. Spectroscopy does not constrain D′∥,nsD^{\prime}_{\parallel,ns}. All couplings are ambient-pressure values; at 2.42.4–2.92.9 GPa the buckling that allows the in-plane components is expected to decrease [71], which would lower T∗T^{*}. The interlayer coupling Jc=0.053​(3)J_{c}=0.053(3) meV≃0.6{}\simeq 0.6 K, fitted at 5.55.5 GPa in the monoclinic antiferromagnet [28] and consistent with Jc=0.049​(6)J_{c}=0.049(6) meV from inelastic neutron data at 4.24.2 GPa [8], exceeds T∗T^{*} and is not included.

  • •

    The window [δ′,λ][\delta^{\prime},\lambda] requires proximity to the critical pressure through the Higgs deviation sHs_{H}, which no measurement fixes. T∗⁣∗≃(0.03CLOSET^{**}\simeq(0.03–OPEN0.1)​λ0.1)\lambda is an order-of-magnitude one-loop estimate at order-one coupling. With dynamical screening, the transverse gauge field and the Higgs polarization included, the gauge interaction alone lies 22–4%4\% of its norm from the boundary between the VBS and chirality basins, and Higgs exchange through the Yukawa coupling crosses it only outside the pseudocritical window. Deep in the Higgsed phase no weak-coupling instability follows, and strong-coupling instabilities of the displaced Dirac phase are not analyzed.

  • •

    The basin fractions of the one-loop flow are scheme-dependent, and the majority verdict is a one-loop statement.

  • •

    The quartic seeds are computed at tree level, of order J′J^{\prime}, and run to λ\lambda with the O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) four-fermion dimensions of Appendix K, a linear running that is not controlled for seeds of that size. The SO(5)-singlet scalar channel is solved at O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) with five operators, Δ1=2.99\Delta_{1}=2.99 (2.912.91 in the physical-NfN_{f} counting), but its Higgs sector is not controlled at N=12N=12, where the constraint field has Δσ=0.38\Delta_{\sigma}=0.38, below the unitarity bound; the two further Higgs operators of the channel decouple at this order, and the Yukawa coupling is not included. Whether the seed linear in D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} or the lattice-determinant term leads the DM correction to the plaquette pattern depends on Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} and on the determinant ratio, and is not established. The sign of D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} is that of the NMR determination of Ref. [63]; the opposite sign read from the far-infrared analysis of Ref. [11] rests on an assumed relative sign of the phonon-induced DM vectors, and Ref. [77] attributes the discrepancy to conventions. The selection that the pure Shastry–Sutherland model makes beyond tree level is not computed. The coefficient AA of Eq. (23) is derived only for the band-touching channel of the determinant, exchange fluctuations beyond the determinant renormalize b2b_{2}, and the Ising transition temperature and order are not computed.

  • •

    The Chern number CBdG=∓4C_{\rm BdG}=\mp 4 holds locally for the Z300011 state, and the PSG class does not fix it. The magnitude of MzM_{z} is not computed, and the thermal Hall quantization assumes a gapped deconfined ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} sector.

  • •

    The field-induced coefficients are Gaussian, fluctuation corrections are not computed, and no moment is quoted in μB\mu_{B}. The dimer-phase moments of Ref. [63] are not identified with a specific channel, which would require a matrix-element calculation.

  • •
